Let’s dive into Chapter 6: Mastering Self-Promotion Without Losing Authenticity.
As you build new habits and grow, there’s a fresh challenge that often pops up. How do you advocate for yourself—and your work—without feeling like you’re bragging or losing that genuine spark?
A lot of women worry that self-promotion will come across as arrogance, or maybe even self-centeredness. But here’s something to keep in mind—being visible really matters if you want to move forward. So, what if you could see self-promotion as a kind of professional storytelling? It’s about sharing your contributions in a way that feels real and truly makes an impact.
Self-promotion isn’t about exaggerating or taking credit for someone else’s hard work. It’s about making sure your efforts are visible to the people who actually make decisions about new opportunities and growth.
Picture a beautiful garden. Only the most colorful flowers get noticed, right? But imagine the most stunning blooms hidden away in the shade—they might never get seen. In the same way, the valuable work you do can be overlooked if you don’t shine a light on it.
So, how do you master self-promotion while staying true to yourself? Here are a few practical ways:
First, try sharing your accomplishments within the bigger picture of your team or organization. For instance, you might say, “I’m proud that my project helped us meet our quarterly targets.”
Next, stick to the facts and results—focus on the impact of what you’ve done, rather than talking about personal traits.
It also helps to practice your “elevator pitch.” Think of short, clear summaries of your recent wins or skills, so they feel natural when they come up in conversation.
And don’t forget to lift up others, too. When you support and recognize your colleagues’ achievements, you help create a culture where everyone’s work gets seen.
Let’s look at a real-life example. Imagine someone on your team led a big initiative, but she feels a bit shy about mentioning it during meetings. If she prepares a quick summary of the project’s results and shares it in a team update, she not only brings her own work to light—she also sets a positive example for everyone else.
Another thing that can really help? Ask for feedback on how your self-promotion comes across. Trusted colleagues or mentors can give you honest insights about your tone and delivery, making it easier to find the right mix of confidence and humility.
The heart of self-promotion is simple: make sure your valuable work gets seen and appreciated. When you approach it with integrity, and keep the focus on shared success, self-promotion becomes a tool for both your own growth and your organization’s progress.
